text: Technology Layer 1 should be tracked as an AI infrastructure stack, not a single software or semiconductor trade: demand originates in AI/cloud workloads and propagates through accelerators, HBM, foundry, packaging, networking, cybersecurity, and power/cooling/grid constraints.

The highest-priority chokepoint lane remains AI accelerators plus HBM plus advanced-node foundry plus advanced packaging, because the bottleneck can migrate across these capacity and qualification layers.

Process control, inspection, metrology, probe cards, and automated test should stay in the funnel because HBM and advanced packaging complexity can make yield learning and qualification a hidden bottleneck.

AI networking and optical interconnect deserve independent treatment from compute accelerators because cluster utilization, latency, bandwidth, and congestion control can constrain the effective value of installed GPUs.

Data-center power, cooling, and grid infrastructure are first-order technology nodes because AI deployment can be constrained by time-to-power, thermal density, interconnection queues, and firm clean-power availability.

Layer 2 should add non-U.S. public suppliers in Korea, Taiwan, Japan, Europe, China, and Hong Kong, especially HBM, substrates, optical modules, advanced packaging equipment, thermal, and power-equipment suppliers.

Layer 2 should convert inference-stage candidates into evidence-ranked candidates using primary filings, investor presentations, customer/qualification evidence, revenue mix, backlog, capex, and market-pricing checks.

For the Technology theme, use AI infrastructure as the current dominant chain unless the next prompt specifies another subtheme such as robotics, cybersecurity, enterprise software, quantum, consumer devices, or biotech tools.
Highest-priority physical chokepoints: advanced packaging, HBM, leading-edge foundry, optical/networking, data-center power/interconnection, and liquid cooling.

Near-term catalysts should be organized around hyperscaler capex updates, TSMC capacity/capex commentary, HBM supplier earnings, NVIDIA platform roadmap/ramp timing, Broadcom custom AI/networking revenue, and DOE/grid/permitting developments.

Need later Layer 2B/3 verification of exact supplier exposure for ABF substrates, interposers, probe cards, liquid-cooling components, power equipment, and optical component vendors before mapping to individual equities.
Need market-pricing check later: determine whether public equities already discount the bottleneck by comparing revenue growth, backlog, gross margin, capex, valuation, and estimate revisions.

NVDA should be treated as the top-level AI platform demand aggregator in this chunk; its Vera Rubin and Blackwell/Rubin deployments drive pull-through demand for HBM, TSMC advanced nodes, advanced packaging, networking, test, power, and cooling.
TSM is the primary capacity bottleneck mapping for leading-edge logic and advanced packaging; Layer 2C should separate wafer-node capacity from CoWoS/3DFabric-style packaging capacity.
MU is the direct U.S.-listed HBM mapping, but the full HBM node remains incomplete without SK hynix and Samsung local tickers and primary filings.
AVGO has primary-source evidence for AI semiconductor revenue driven by custom AI accelerators and AI networking, making it a high-priority non-GPU AI compute/networking relationship.
ONTO, TER, and FORM are increasingly important hidden-bottleneck mappings because AI/HBM ramps raise inspection, metrology, automated test, and probe-card intensity.

AMKR is the key U.S.-listed OSAT/advanced-packaging mapping in this chunk, but its true chokepoint status depends on whether it captures high-end AI heterogeneous integration programs versus lower-complexity packaging volume.
ASML relationship is structurally strong but needs a current primary-source bridge from AI/HBM/leading-edge capacity additions to EUV/High-NA order intake, shipment timing, and bottleneck status.
ANET requires more granular evidence on AI-specific revenue mix, 800G/1.6T transition exposure, customer concentration, and whether optics/switch-silicon constraints affect shipments or margins.

AMD needs shipment-level validation for MI350/MI450 and rack-scale systems; headline gigawatt or strategic partnership announcements should not be treated as realized revenue without delivery schedules and capacity evidence.
KLAC needs segment-level validation separating AI-related advanced packaging, HBM, and leading-edge logic process-control demand from broader wafer-fab equipment cyclicality.

In this candidate chunk, AMAT, MRVL, COHR, LITE, ENTG, and LRCX are closer to Serenity-style physical supply-chain bottlenecks than MSFT, GOOGL, AMZN, META, ORCL, and SNOW, which are mainly demand aggregators or monetization layers.

AMAT has the strongest explicit AI semicap evidence in this chunk because current 2026 materials tie leading-edge foundry-logic, DRAM/HBM, and advanced packaging to AI performance-per-watt and WFE growth.

MRVL has strong direct mapping to AI optical interconnect and custom silicon through 1.6T optical DSPs, coherent DCI products, and AI data-center connectivity positioning; future work should separate optical DSP, custom XPU, Ethernet, and DCI revenue drivers.
COHR and LITE are optical-component candidates where bottleneck status depends on AI datacom mix, 800G/1.6T qualification, InP/laser capacity, yields, and hyperscaler/NVIDIA-linked customer evidence.

MSFT, GOOGL, AMZN, META, and ORCL should be tracked as capex and cloud-demand validators; their relationship to the theme is strongest when capex commitments, capacity constraints, and AI workload monetization pull through demand to accelerators, HBM, optics, networking, power, and data-center construction.

SNOW belongs to the enterprise AI data layer, not the physical compute chokepoint layer; its research question is whether AI Data Cloud products create incremental consumption and retention rather than only thematic positioning.
Need primary-source validation for ENTG's AI-specific exposure: quantify revenue or management commentary tied to HBM, EUV, advanced nodes, advanced packaging, and contamination-control demand.
Need LRCX FY2026 earnings-call evidence distinguishing AI-related HBM/DRAM/foundry/advanced-packaging tool demand from broader wafer-fab equipment cyclicality and China/export-control exposure.

Need customer-level or segment-level evidence for COHR and LITE to test whether optics demand is capacity-constrained and margin-accretive, or vulnerable to hyperscaler inventory cycles and price pressure.
Need market-pricing check in a later layer: compare expected AI revenue/capex growth versus current valuation and consensus assumptions without producing buy/sell recommendations or price targets.

DDOG should be tracked as an AI production observability and security operations platform: useful for AI workload complexity, GPU monitoring, MCP/agent access, and LLM operations, but not a hard supply bottleneck unless AI observability becomes mission-critical and differentiated.
NOW should be tracked as an enterprise AI workflow and agent-governance platform, with thesis quality dependent on incremental AI ACV, attach rates, and realized workflow automation value.

PANW, CRWD, and ZS map to AI/cloud security enablement; their Serenity priority should depend on evidence that AI deployments create new security budget rather than merely re-labeling normal platform consolidation.

VRT is the strongest physical-infrastructure bottleneck candidate in this chunk because high-density AI deployment directly stresses power and cooling systems and Vertiv has explicit AI data-center power/cooling evidence.

ETN maps to electrical power-management infrastructure for AI data centers and should be tested through order growth, backlog duration, switchgear/transformer capacity, and AI-factory architecture disclosures.

PWR maps to grid interconnection and large-load execution rather than data-center equipment; its bottleneck value depends on skilled-labor scarcity, utility backlog, and large-load project conversion.

CEG maps to firm low-carbon power supply and potential data-center co-location; key validation is signed data-center PPAs, regulatory approval, and whether co-location economics survive policy scrutiny.
SMR remains speculative for AI data-center power because evidence supports advanced nuclear thematic relevance but not near-term AI data-center deployment certainty.

ARM has a clearer AI compute-architecture relationship than most software names in this chunk because FY2026 disclosures cite data-center royalty growth and Cloud AI, but it is still an IP/architecture lever rather than a capacity bottleneck.
INTC should remain hypothesis-stage until external foundry, advanced packaging, and AI/HPC customer ramps are proven with volumes, revenues, and yields rather than technology roadmaps alone.
Need primary earnings-call transcripts and segment-level data for DDOG, NOW, PANW, CRWD, and ZS to separate AI-specific incremental revenue from broader software and cybersecurity growth.

Need backlog, lead-time, capacity-expansion, and pricing evidence for VRT, ETN, and PWR to confirm whether power/cooling/grid nodes are genuine chokepoints or simply high-growth but competitive infrastructure markets.
Need customer-level power-contract evidence for CEG and project-level deployment evidence for SMR before assigning high-confidence AI power-supply exposure.
Need ARM customer deployment details and INTC external foundry/package revenue conversion to assess whether compute architecture optionality translates into durable economic capture.
